fixes.explanation: True, baker, you spotted the pattern. At the entrance to the Tent of Meeting, the man lays his hand on the head of his peace offering and slaughters it (Leviticus 3:2). The burnt offering began with a hand on the head too (Leviticus 1:4). After that, Aaron's sons the priests splatter the blood on all sides of the altar.

Deer and gazelles never make the list, friend. The LORD says the animal comes “…from the herd or the flock.” (Leviticus 1:2) Sheep or goats make up the flock (Leviticus 1:10), and a burnt offering of birds can be a turtledove or a young pigeon (Leviticus 1:14). Chasing a gazelle across the hills sounds like a very long way to go for a drop-off.

Yes, friend. The text says, “…Aaron’s sons the priests are to present the blood and splatter it on all sides of the altar at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting.” (Leviticus 1:5) The man has his own jobs, like slaughtering the young bull before the LORD. Presenting and splattering the blood is the priests' work.

All of it goes up, friend. First the animal is skinned and cut into pieces (Leviticus 1:6), and the entrails and legs are washed. Then the text says, “…the priest shall burn all of it on the altar as a burnt offering…” (Leviticus 1:9) Everything laid on that altar gets burned, with nothing held back.

That's right. The text says, “He shall tear it open by its wings, without dividing the bird completely.” (Leviticus 1:17) The head has already been twisted off (Leviticus 1:15) and the crop removed (Leviticus 1:16), so this bird isn't whole anymore. But it isn't split in two either. Then the priest burns it on the altar atop the burning wood.

Correct, baker! The handful goes up in smoke as the memorial portion, and the rest belongs to Aaron and his sons, who are the priests (Leviticus 1:5). The text calls it “…a most holy part of the food offerings to the LORD.” (Leviticus 2:3) In my kitchen, leftover dough goes to whoever sneaks in first. Here, it has a clear owner.

Nice try, friend, but the man doesn't take it home. The text says the remainder “…shall belong to Aaron and his sons…” (Leviticus 2:3), and those are the priests (Leviticus 1:5). I bet it feels odd to hand over a batch you worked on and not carry any back. But that's how this one goes.

A next-morning burning isn't anywhere in this passage, friend. The handful is what goes up in smoke, as the memorial portion. The remainder “…shall belong to Aaron and his sons…” (Leviticus 2:3), who are the priests (Leviticus 1:5). Nobody's setting an alarm to torch leftovers.

Leaven is one of the two, baker. The verse says, “…you are not to burn any leaven or honey as a food offering to the LORD.” (Leviticus 2:11) That's why the oven versions are unleavened cakes and unleavened wafers (Leviticus 2:4). Bakers love a good rise, but leaven sits this one out.

True! The text says, “You may bring them to the LORD as an offering of firstfruits, but they must not go up on the altar as a pleasing aroma.” (Leviticus 2:12) So leaven and honey do have a place as firstfruits. They just don't go up on the altar. Good catch on that “as long as,” baker.

Careful, friend, that one's true, and it's easy to trip on. The verse starts, “You may bring them to the LORD as an offering of firstfruits…” (Leviticus 2:12) So leaven and honey are allowed as firstfruits. The only no is the altar, since they “…must not go up on the altar as a pleasing aroma.”

Both halves check out, baker, and you didn't even blink. The firstfruits grain gets oil and frankincense (Leviticus 2:15). Then the priest burns the memorial portion of the crushed grain and the oil, together with all its frankincense (Leviticus 2:16). Keep that pattern in your head and the next one gets easier.
